title: Name release tags so the history explains itself
tagline: branch-A.B.C: which environment, which phase, which release, which fix.
intro: A tag marks the exact commit that was shipped. With one naming rule, anyone can read off where and what was released without opening a ticket.

sections.title: Overview
sections.summary: Four parts, each answering one question.

blocks.caption: Reading dev-2.3.1 from left to right.

items.label: branch
items.detail: The branch the build came from, which is also the environment it went to
explain: dev-… went to the dev environment, prod-… to production. Two tags on one commit are fine: a build promoted to prod keeps its dev tag.
git tag --list 'prod-*' is then the full release history of production, in one command.

items.label: A — phase
items.detail: The project phase; it goes up when a new contract phase or major scope starts
explain: Phase 2 of a project starts at dev-2.0.0, whatever the last tag of phase 1 was.
Raising A resets both B and C, because the earlier releases belong to the previous phase.

items.label: B — release
items.detail: A planned release within the phase: a new batch of features
explain: dev-2.3.0 is the third planned release of phase 2 after 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2.
Raising B resets C to 0, since the fixes counted so far were fixes to the previous release.

items.label: C — fix
items.detail: Counts rebuilds of the same release; resets to 0 whenever A or B goes up
explain: dev-2.3.1 is the first fix build of release 2.3. Another fix makes it dev-2.3.2.
So C = 0 if A or B increased, otherwise C = C + 1. That single rule keeps the numbers unambiguous.

blocks.caption: An annotated tag records who tagged it and when

body: The store build number is separate: bump it on every Android or iOS release, but leave it out of the tag.
